doc.title: Ruth Brown interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Accompanying a singer and the black church
summary: Brown and the interviewer discuss the special skill of accompanying a singer, found in the black church, and singing from the heart.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: And yet support. And you can’t always find that.
It’s a special skill, isn’t it.
That’s it. It’s a special skill.
Now you tell me am I wrong where I’ve found the greatest accompanist for singers is in the black church.

Oh why of course. Of course. Because we’re not in a hurry. And that’s what I tell everybody. Where you going? Take your time. Slow down. Listen to what you’re saying. Not only should it feed off and affect somebody else, it should feed back on you. It’s like looking in the mirror, you know? You used to always look in the mirror when you talk to yourself, because it’s going to feed back on you. You see and you will feel it. Same way with your music. If you sing it, and it’s heartfelt, you’ll get that too. I’ve been on stage sometime and some nights are different than others. You know you can focus on someone in your audience and get really locked into them, you know you get eye contact and you realize that they’re really listening to what you’re singing. And before you know it, you’re hearing yourself. As I’ve said in my, I call it my older days, in my twilight years I’ve started to collect and listen to some of my recordings. I never did listen to my own stuff that much. But I started to listen to some of it now. Some of it’s pretty good. But some of it is awful. You know.
